title: Disability, accommodation, assistive technology, and contextual correction

observations.claim: EEOC guidance gives an example in which a keystroke-based productivity algorithm could disadvantage a blind worker using voice-recognition software.
limits: Illustrative guidance, not a named case finding.

observations.claim: EEOC and DOJ warn that software and AI used for monitoring, pay, promotion and other employment decisions can create ADA screen-out risk.
limits: No named deployment misuse is established.

observations.claim: EEOC guidance recommends explaining how technology evaluates workers and providing an accommodation path.
limits: Promising practice language is retained as guidance.

observations.claim: ICO monitoring guidance requires accuracy controls and says workers should be able to see, explain and challenge monitoring results used in adverse decisions.
limits: UK guidance under review; no case judgment.

observations.claim: ICO biometric guidance requires manual review pathways and rapid restoration where automated access denial could cause lost pay or discipline.
The Platform Work Directive bars automated inference of disability and health status and requires safety and psychosocial risk assessment.
limits: Platform-work scope and transposition boundary remain explicit.

findings.claim: A low activity or speed score can encode a tool, interface or disability mismatch rather than lower job capacity.
limits: No individual diagnosis or named causal conclusion.

findings.claim: Accommodation must attach before adverse use of the metric; equal administration does not establish equal construct measurement.
limits: Exact legal duties remain jurisdiction- and fact-specific.

findings.claim: Manual correction is meaningful only if it can restore access, pay, opportunity and the underlying record before downstream discipline propagates.
The worker-facing receipt should retain assistive technology, accommodation request, intended construct, disposition and alternative evidence as separate fields.
